stem:
What does this NumPy code produce?

import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(arr * 2)
explanation_after: NumPy applies operations element-wise. Multiplying an array by 2 doubles every element simultaneously. This is called vectorisation — much faster than a Python for-loop.

stem: Why is NumPy faster than regular Python for math operations?

options.text: NumPy operations run in optimised C code and operate on entire arrays at once
NumPy uses a faster version of Python
NumPy only works with small numbers

explanation_after: NumPy's core is written in C, a compiled language much faster than Python. It also avoids Python loops entirely by operating on whole arrays at once. This is why PyTorch and TensorFlow are built on similar principles.

stem:
What is the shape of this NumPy array?

arr = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
explanation_after: This is a 2D array with 2 rows and 3 columns. Shape = (rows, columns) = (2, 3). Understanding shapes is critical — shape mismatches cause most beginner errors in deep learning.

options.text: A generalisation of arrays to any number of dimensions
A special type of neural network

explanation_after: A scalar is 0D (single number). A vector is 1D. A matrix is 2D. A tensor is the general term for N-dimensional arrays. PyTorch's core object is a Tensor — essentially NumPy with GPU support and automatic differentiation.

stem:
What does this code output?

import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a + b)
explanation_after: NumPy broadcasting stretches the smaller array (shape (3,)) across each row of the larger array (shape (2,3)) without actually copying data, adding it element-wise to every row. Broadcasting is what lets you add a bias vector to every row of a batch of activations in a neural network without writing an explicit loop.

stem: Why does training a neural network on a batch of 256 images at once (as a single (256, 784) array) run dramatically faster than looping through the 256 images one at a time in Python?

options.text: Because batching skips some of the images to save time
Because a vectorised array operation runs as optimised, parallelised low-level code, avoiding the overhead of 256 separate Python-level loop iterations
Because a batch of 256 images takes up less memory than 256 individual images
Because Python automatically converts loops into batches with no other benefit

explanation_after: Each iteration of a Python for-loop carries interpreter overhead. A vectorised operation on a (256, 784) array dispatches a single call into optimised C/CUDA code that processes all 256 rows in parallel, especially on a GPU. This is exactly why deep learning trains on batches — it's not just a stability trick, it's what makes the underlying matrix math fast enough to train at all.
